sentence: I am uneasy about this film, and the unease is not a criticism so much as a description of what the picture is for. It takes a subject most people would prefer not to think about and refuses to let the audience look away, and the discomfort I felt was plainly intended. A film about this material that left me comfortable would have failed. This one succeeds, if success is the word, by being almost unbearable.

The film's central sequence — a forty-minute traversal of a mountain village in a single autumn afternoon — is one of the most beautiful pieces of animated filmmaking I have seen in years. The light shifts believably as the day moves. The villagers, none of them named, go about their work and contribute incidentally to the story. There is no dialogue at all for the middle twenty minutes, and yet the picture is more emotionally engaged in that silence than most live-action films are at full volume.

The film addresses a subject that has become almost impossible to address without controversy, and it does so with a clear-eyed sobriety that I found admirable. It does not editorialise. It does not soften. It presents its difficult material with a documentary steadiness and trusts the audience to bring their own conscience to it, and that trust is, in the current climate, an act of genuine artistic nerve.

The performance is uncanny — accent, gait, even the way he lights a cigarette — and yet the film around it never adds up to a portrait. Biopics of famously private people often end up with this problem, where the more accurately the impersonation lands, the more obvious it becomes that we have no real access to the inner life it points at. I left admiring the craft and unsure what I had learned.

Another music biopic in the standard shape — the early gig, the breakthrough, the slide into addiction, the reconciliation with the estranged parent. The lead does an honest impersonation, and the wardrobe department has earned its budget, but you can see every story beat coming from the trailer, and the film never finds a reason to be more than a competent dramatisation of facts already covered in better books.

subtopic: screen adaptation of a stage play
sentence: The film preserves the play's text almost intact, and the text was always the source's great strength, so the picture inherits a real verbal richness. The trouble is the staging, which is so reverent that the camera barely moves for two hours, and the cumulative effect is closer to a recorded performance than a film. The performances are the kind of full-throated theatrical work that plays beautifully from the stalls and lands slightly too large in close-up. It is worth seeing. It is not, quite, a film.

This is a brave, untidy documentary that refuses to pretend it has solved the case at the heart of it. The filmmakers admit on screen that some of their sources have lied to them, that other doors have been closed, and that the editing process itself has shaped the conclusions you are about to reach. Watching them grapple with that honestly is more compelling than any tidy non-fiction thriller would have been.

subtopic: the studio film with troubled production history
sentence: The studio has released the film quietly, hoping, one assumes, that nobody will connect it to the two years of bad press about its making, and the strategy is futile, because the production history is the most interesting thing about the picture. The film itself is a bland, broken-backed compromise. The story of how it got broken is genuinely dramatic, and somebody should make a documentary about that instead.

There is a long sequence in this western, a cattle drive across a drought-stricken plain, that contains some of the most extraordinary natural-light photography I have seen in years. The director has waited, evidently for weeks, for exactly the right skies, and the patience is visible in every frame. The story the film is telling is a familiar one of revenge and reluctant redemption, but the picture is worth seeing for the landscape work alone, which is the kind of cinema the western was invented to make possible.

I cannot in good conscience call this picture a good film and I would also cheerfully watch it again. The creature suit is magnificent. The screenplay is, in places, unintentionally hilarious. The lead is doing the kind of work that should disqualify a performer from serious roles and which has, on the contrary, only enhanced his cult standing. The picture's principal flaw is that it ends, and I suspect that is the most generous thing one can say about a B-movie in this year of cinema.

The trouble with an ensemble piece this large is that the screenplay has roughly nine minutes for each of its many characters, and nine minutes is not enough to build a person. The film introduces a dozen lives, sketches each in a few broad strokes, and then asks us to be moved when their paths cross. We are not moved, because we do not know them, and the picture's busy structure has mistaken the quantity of characters for the richness of a world.

subtopic: screen adaptation of a stage play
sentence: The single greatest pleasure of this adaptation is watching the original stage cast, all of whom have been retained, perform material they have plainly inhabited for years. There is a lived-in ease to the ensemble work that no newly assembled film cast could replicate. The director has wisely stepped back and let them work, and the camera's principal job is simply to be in the right place to catch the looks that pass between actors who have done this scene three hundred times.

What this hybrid film understands is that genre is a set of expectations, and that expectations can be played like an instrument. The picture invokes the conventions of the heist movie and then, having earned the audience's anticipation, quietly redirects it into the register of a grief drama, and the redirection itself becomes the source of feeling. It is a sophisticated game, and the film plays it with a control that more single-minded pictures rarely achieve.

The jukebox musical has, in recent years, become a kind of greatest-hits delivery vehicle wrapped in a perfunctory plot. This one is no exception. The songs are arranged in roughly the order an algorithm would suggest, the dialogue between them is the connective tissue of a poorly written biographical drama, and the dancing is competent in the way that a corporate event's entertainment is competent. The audience the morning I saw it knew every word, and clapped along, and left smiling. Make of that what you will.

The picture's use of silence is its boldest musical decision. The composer was apparently instructed to write a full score and then, in the edit, the director removed nearly all of it, leaving the film's most harrowing sequences to play out in total quiet. The absence is devastating. We are denied the orchestral cushion that would tell us how to feel, and forced to sit with the images unguided, and the discomfort is precisely the point. A score, sometimes, is most powerful when it has been taken away.

The picture is, in the technical sense, a self-portrait. The protagonist is a filmmaker of roughly the director's age, working through roughly the director's recent personal disasters, and the temptation to read it as confession is hard to resist. The film knows this, and the more interesting question it asks is what kind of confession it is — whether the camera is being used to tell the truth or to organise the surroundings until they look like one. The answer it offers is not flattering.

The picture is built on a single destabilising question, and the director is disciplined enough never to answer it. We are never told whether the protagonist's mounting paranoia is justified or symptomatic, and the film makes us live inside that uncertainty for two hours. It would be an unbearable trick if the lead performance were not so calibrated, holding the line between victim and unreliable narrator without ever tipping the audience off. By the closing scene I trusted nothing, including my own attention, which is exactly where the film wanted me.

subtopic: child performance and family film reviews
sentence: The picture is a family film with the rare courage to be sad. It is about a child's first encounter with death, the death of a grandparent, and it does not rush the child through grief toward a tidy lesson. It lets the sadness sit. The young lead's performance is remarkable precisely because the director has not asked her to perform sadness but simply to be present within it, and the film earns its eventual, modest consolation honestly.

The picture finally locates a fresh angle on a tired form by setting the heist inside an organisation the crew themselves work for. The protagonist's quiet moral negotiation — robbing the firm he has spent twenty years inside — is the dramatic centre, and the screenplay treats the heist itself almost as the side issue. The film is unfashionably interested in the consequences. The third-act audit-and-investigation material, which most heist films skip entirely, is here the strongest of the film.

The film is a western set in the genre's twilight, the early years of the new century, when the railways and the fences had begun to close the frontier, and the picture is suffused with a sense of an era ending. The aging gunfighter at its centre is a man whose entire skill set has become obsolete, and the film treats his irrelevance with a tenderness that the genre's harder revisions usually withhold. It is an elegy, and a genuinely moving one.

The folk-horror revival continues to produce films that mistake atmosphere for plot. There are wide shots of standing stones, there is a slowly building drumbeat, there are villagers who do not blink, and there is a young protagonist who does not believe the warnings until it's too late. We have seen all of these before, and we have seen them done better, and the new film does not have a fresh idea of its own to add to the assembly.

I went in braced for the worst and came out won over. The premise is hoary, the structure is familiar, and the trailer had given away what looked like every joke. But the picture has a secret weapon, which is a supporting cast given real material instead of the usual disposable comic relief, and the world around the central couple feels genuinely populated. The romance works because it is happening among people we have come to care about, and the film is the rare romantic comedy with a functioning ensemble.

It is a familiar disappointment, the film that cannot land its ending, and this picture is a particularly painful instance because the first two acts are so good. The director has clearly understood the human material beautifully and the plot mechanics not at all, and the third act is all plot mechanics, a clattering apparatus of twists and reversals grinding toward a resolution that satisfies the diagram and betrays the people.

Another procession of jump scares pretending to be a film. The director has clearly seen better horror pictures and assumed that imitating their imagery would do the work of imitating their tension. It does not. The cast is fine, the production design is appropriately damp and grey, and the score is doing everything the script refuses to do, which is to keep us interested. By the midpoint I had stopped flinching, which in a horror film is a kind of small death.

The remake exists for no reason that the film itself can articulate. It reproduces the original's plot beat for beat, updates the technology, recasts the roles with current stars, and adds nothing, asks nothing, discovers nothing. The original was not a flawed film waiting to be improved; it was a complete one. This new version is a competent photocopy, and watching it I felt the particular melancholy of seeing something I loved repeated by people who did not understand why it had worked.

The film about the occupied village is exactly as morally serious as it should be, and exactly as cinematic. The screenplay refuses every easy reveal — there is no last-minute heroism, no convenient resistance breakout, no final defiant speech — and yet the picture never becomes flat. The performances are pitched at a register of held breath, sustained for two hours, and the cumulative effect is more moving than any louder film could have managed.

The picture has been shot almost entirely in extreme close-up, and the choice, sustained for two hours, becomes genuinely oppressive. We are never permitted to see a room, a landscape, a body in full; we are pressed against faces and hands and fragments for the entire running time. I understand the intention, an intimacy bordering on suffocation, and for twenty minutes it is effective. For two hours it is a punishment, and I left the cinema craving the simple relief of a wide shot.

The picture has been built, sensibly, as a showcase for its veteran star, and the star repays the gift completely. This is late-career work of a high order, a performance that uses the actor's age and history as instruments rather than apologising for them. The character is meant to be a man at the end of something, and the performer brings to that ending a gravity that no amount of makeup or writing could have manufactured.

What is missing from most adolescent films is the boredom, and that is what this picture restores. The long afternoons in which absolutely nothing happens are filmed at the length they actually occupy in a young person's life. The director understands that boredom is not the absence of plot but a particular kind of emotional pressure, and her willingness to film it patiently is what makes the eventual small events feel as enormous as they would feel at that age.

subtopic: silent film and early cinema reviews
sentence: The new score commissioned for this 1916 restoration is, regrettably, the worst thing about the screening. The composer has written a relentlessly busy accompaniment that insists on underlining every moment, and the film's images, which are perfectly capable of speaking for themselves, are smothered. Silent cinema at its best leaves room for the audience's own attention. This score fills every silence, and the picture, paradoxically, becomes harder to hear.

The picture is ostensibly about a marathon runner, but its real subject is obsession, and the director has the courage to make that obsession genuinely unappealing. The protagonist is not a likeable striver; she is a difficult, narrow, frequently cruel person whose single-mindedness costs everyone around her. The film does not soften this, and it does not punish it either. It simply observes, with great precision, the price of being extraordinary at one thing, and the observation is bracing.

This is the rare prestige drama that earns its slow burn. The director resists the temptation to underline her themes and instead lets the camera linger on small refusals — a hand half-raised, a dinner gone cold. The two central performances are extraordinary in opposite ways, one all surface composure, the other all interior weather. By the time the final scene arrives, the picture has accumulated a quiet authority that more strident films would envy.

subtopic: silent film and early cinema reviews
sentence: The picture is an early trick film, barely twelve minutes long, and it has survived precisely because it was never thought important enough to be worth destroying. Watching it now, the modern viewer can see the entire grammar of cinema being invented in real time, the filmmaker discovering, shot by shot, that a cut can move us through space, that a closer view can direct our attention. It is less a film than a record of a medium teaching itself to think, and it is enthralling.

The festival chose to close on this picture, and the choice tells you everything about the festival's mood this year. It is a warm, well-mannered crowd-pleaser, the kind of film designed to send a tired audience out into the night feeling that the week of difficult cinema had a point. The performances are charming, the resolution is tidy, and I enjoyed it precisely as much as I was meant to and not one degree more.

Another coming-of-age picture about a sensitive boy and his slightly older female friend. The casting is good, the period detail is fine, and the protagonist's narration is just self-aware enough to be irritating without being self-aware enough to step out of the trope it is occupying. The film does nothing actively wrong, which is itself the problem — there is no reason for this picture to exist that I could deduce from watching it, and the genre has had quite enough of its kind recently.

The film cost almost nothing to make, and it would be patronising to praise it merely for that. So let me be clear, this is not a good film for its budget, it is a good film, full stop, and the budget is simply an irrelevant fact about its making. The screenplay is excellent. The performances are excellent. The picture would be a triumph at any price, and it happens, also, to have been a bargain.

The 1830s parlour scenes are staged with such confident period detail that you stop noticing the corsetry and start hearing the conversations. The director resists the temptation to modernise the dialogue. Sentences are long and slightly overformal, the way they would have been, and the actors are clearly enjoying the chance to think inside that rhythm. The picture's politics are sharper than its surface suggests, and the closing image — a letter unfolding in a stranger's hand — earns the weight it is asked to carry.

subtopic: screen adaptation of a stage play
sentence: The director has done the unthinkable and improved on a celebrated play, largely by trusting the camera to find what the stage could only gesture at. The pivotal scene, which on stage relied on a character described offstage, is here finally shown, and the showing transforms the meaning of everything around it. Purists will object. They will be wrong. This is what a screen adaptation should be: not a recording of a play but a genuine rethinking of it for a medium that can do different things.

There are two excellent practical creature effects in this film, both in service of a screenplay that does not deserve them. The monster, when it finally appears in full light, is one of the more inventive designs I have seen in years, and the puppeteers should be on awards lists. But the script around the creature is a clutter of underwritten teenagers running between locations, and no amount of latex and rod-puppetry can rescue a third act this confused.

subtopic: the film that improves on a second viewing
sentence: I am writing this review after a second viewing, because my first response was so different that I no longer trust it. What had seemed cold and withholding now seems precise and disciplined. What had seemed like an anticlimax now seems like the only honest ending available. The film is the same film. I have simply learned, on the return, how to watch it, and the lesson was worth the rewatch.

The picture proves, yet again, a truth the industry seems determined to forget, that the relationship between a film's budget and its quality is essentially nil. This tiny film, made by unknowns for the price of a modest car, is funnier, sadder, and more memorable than the bloated tentpole I reviewed last week. The money buys spectacle. It cannot buy the things that actually matter, and this small triumph is the proof.

The film is visually incoherent in a way that suggests a production with no controlling eye. Some scenes are lit with care; others appear to have been shot with whatever was available. The colour grading shifts without motivation. The framing is sometimes precise and sometimes careless. A film can have an ugly visual style and still be unified, but this picture has no style at all, only a sequence of visual decisions made, scene by scene, by people who were not consulting one another.

The casting director should receive a credit above the title. This ensemble piece works almost entirely because every role, down to the smallest, has been filled by exactly the right face and voice, and the film generates a great deal of its pleasure simply from the rightness of its people. The screenplay is solid without being exceptional. The direction is unobtrusive. But the gathered cast has a collective texture, a sense of having been chosen with real care, and it carries the whole film.

The mockumentary form has been so thoroughly worked over by television that a feature-length entry now has to do something distinctive, and this picture barely tries. The handheld camera, the awkward pauses, the talking-to-camera asides — all of these are deployed exactly as they have been in a thousand previous productions, and the laughs largely depend on the audience recognising the form rather than discovering anything new. The cast is talented. The script is tired. The combination is a passable evening, no more.

The film unfolds in long, patient takes across a single coastal village over the course of one summer, and almost nothing happens in the conventional sense. What does happen is the slow surfacing of a buried argument between a brother and a sister, and the way the landscape begins to feel like the third party to that argument. It's a film made of weather and silence, and it earns both.

It is genuinely thrilling to watch a film succeed on resourcefulness alone. This picture had no money for a second take, no money for a crane, no money for anything but the bare essentials, and the bare essentials, it turns out, were enough. The director and her tiny crew have made something that feels complete and confident and entirely uncompromised, and they have done it on a budget that would embarrass a wedding video.

The festival has closed on a film by one of its perennial favourites, and the choice has the comfortable feel of a programmer rewarding an old friend. The picture is recognisably the director's work, competent and unsurprising, and the gala audience received it with the warm, slightly dutiful applause reserved for a known quantity. It was a pleasant evening. It was not, by any measure, an event.

The picture has every marker of the awards contender, and watching it is a slightly eerie experience, like meeting a person assembled from a checklist. Here is the historical importance. Here is the social relevance. Here is the showcase monologue, lit and framed for the highlight reel. The film is competent at every individual thing it does, and the sum of all that competence is a strange hollowness, a film that exists to be honoured rather than seen.

The score, built almost entirely from processed and manipulated recordings of the human voice, is the most genuinely original film music I have encountered in a long time. The composer has refused the orchestra, refused the synthesiser, and constructed an entire sonic world from breath and hum and wordless singing. The effect is uncanny and intimate, and it gives the picture a texture no conventional score could provide. It is worth seeing the film for the sound alone.

The screenplay is from a former prosecutor, and you can feel that on screen at every level. The procedural details are correct in a way that legal dramas rarely bother to get correct, the small dynamics of objection and ruling have the rhythm of real proceedings, and the way the witnesses look as they enter the room is, for once, accurate. The film is so steeped in the actual texture of practice that the dramatic engine is doing less work than usual, which I count as a virtue.

There is so much to admire in this film that its third-act collapse is genuinely painful to report. The screenplay, so precise and patient through its opening, simply disintegrates in the final reel into a series of contrivances, the long-lost letter, the timely confession, the coincidental meeting. The film had been better than this. It had spent two acts proving it was better than this, and then, at the finish, it settled.

The film wants very badly to be uncategorisable, and the wanting is the problem. You can feel the screenplay straining to surprise, swerving between tones not because the story demands it but because the writers are terrified of being pinned down. Genuine genre-blending arises from the material; this is genre-blending imposed on the material, and the seams show, and the picture feels less daring than nervous.

Most courtroom films are about the trial. This one is about the discovery period. We spend most of the running time in offices and small windowless conference rooms watching junior associates assemble exhibits, and the picture is unexpectedly gripping. The director has understood that the dramatic mechanics of preparation are at least as compelling as those of performance, and a quietly bureaucratic film about who collects which document and when is, in her hands, a small revelation.

The fake documentary about the fake celebrity is, of course, also a satire of real documentary-making about real celebrities, and at its best the picture is operating on both levels at once. The interview-shot lighting is correctly bad. The archival footage is correctly grainy. The talking-head subjects are correctly self-aggrandising. The picture is so committed to the form's habits that the underlying joke about how these documentaries are made is, by the end, sharper than any of the celebrity-focused gags.

The film is the season's designated important picture, and the designation has done it no favours. You can feel the weight of expectation pressing down on every frame, the sense of a film straining to be worthy, and the strain has squeezed out the spontaneity that the same director's smaller, unheralded work possesses in abundance. The contender is impressive. It is also, somehow, less alive than the films nobody is campaigning for.

The picture is intelligent about a great many things and finally undone by its ending. For most of its length it is a genuinely unnerving study of a man who cannot tell whether he is being gaslit or simply losing his grip, and the ambiguity is held with real skill. Then the screenplay panics, and the final ten minutes deliver a brisk, literal explanation that resolves every question the film had so carefully kept open. It is the sound of a film losing faith in itself at the last possible moment.

The reception at the festival was unusually fractious, and on a second viewing I begin to understand why. The picture is the kind of polemic that mistakes provocation for argument, and reasonable viewers were always going to disagree about whether the film's bad-faith readings of its own characters were an intentional rhetorical move or a structural failure of empathy. I find myself more on the latter side than I did watching it the first time, when the surface tension of the picture briefly carried me.

There's a long monologue about an avocado in the middle of this film that is one of the most sustained comic riffs I've seen in years, and it's almost worth the price of admission on its own. The picture around it is shaggier than it needs to be, and the romantic subplot is a structural afterthought, but in a year of cautious studio comedies, I'll take a film willing to risk a four-minute speech about fruit.

The fake nature documentary about an entirely invented species of burrowing nocturnal mammal is a small triumph of design and performance. The narrator's voice is calibrated almost exactly to the register of every legitimate wildlife documentary I have ever watched. The supposed behavioural footage, generated by some combination of patient practical animation and very careful CGI, is convincing in the way of a magic trick. The film is silly in the best way, which is to say silly and rigorous at the same time.

The new picture from the Iranian director who has been working in exile for the last decade is, as expected, smuggled into being and as a consequence somewhat irregular in technical assembly. The picture is luminous anyway. Shot largely in apartments and at night, on equipment that clearly had to be portable, it accomplishes a moral seriousness that most lavishly resourced festival pictures cannot match. The film is a quiet rebuke to the comforts of how movies usually get made.

The film attempts to render an international tribunal with the kind of intimate dramatic charge that the form usually denies them, and on this it largely succeeds. The translators in the booths get their own subplot. The clerks become characters. The actual proceedings are filmed with the patience required to show the slow accumulation of meaning across days of testimony. It is a more ambitious courtroom film than its mid-range release indicates, and I suspect it will gather a devoted audience in retrospect.

The numbers themselves are uniformly excellent. The choreography is inventive without being showy, the lyrics are dense enough to reward a second listen, and the leads have the rare gift of actually selling a song through the camera rather than merely past it. The connective dialogue scenes are weaker — the writers seem keen to get back to the next musical sequence as quickly as possible — but in a genre this hard to land at feature length, an evening of mostly thrilling numbers is a real achievement.

There is a kind of structural film that builds its meaning from a strict formal system, and this picture announces its system in the first minute and then executes it with relentless discipline for the next seventy. Each shot is exactly four seconds long. Each cut moves one step further along a journey through a single building. The pleasure, and there is real pleasure here, is in watching a rigid constraint generate unexpected emotion, and the film delivers it.

Two hours of beautiful nonsense. The world-building is gorgeous — the floating arcologies, the bioluminescent rain, the bureaucratic forms that govern movement between cities — and the screenplay has clearly thought a great deal about each of them in isolation. What it has not thought about is the actual plot, which is a chase across these landscapes for an object the film never bothers to make us care about. By the third act, the world is the only thing left to look at.

What I admired most about this first feature is its modesty. The young director has resisted every temptation to announce herself, every showy camera move and clever transition that a debut so often uses to demand attention. Instead she has made a small, patient, observant film about a single family, and she has trusted the material to register. It is an unfashionable kind of debut, quiet and assured, and it suggests a long career rather than a brief one.

Adult animation continues to be a category most studios cannot quite figure out how to market, and this strange, beautiful film will probably suffer for that. It is animated to look like a moving graphic novel, with thick black lines and watercolour washes, and it tells a story about a divorce that I do not think live action could have rendered as elegantly. The animation is doing something the writing alone could not, which is the only good reason to make an animated film of an adult subject.

The new feature from the studio that defined a generation of family animation is the most cynical thing they have ever produced. The character designs are recycled from three previous films, the score is the same composer doing roughly the same job, and the screenplay is the kind of safe inter-generational reassurance that nobody actually needs to be told. There are flashes of the old craft in the backgrounds. The hearts of the people in the foregrounds have, for this one, been allowed to clock off early.

The picture is the first installment of a planned trilogy, and it shows, in all the ways that phrase has come to dread. The film is structurally a prologue, three hours of setup for stories that have not yet been told, and it ends not with a conclusion but with a promise. The world is richly imagined and the cast is strong, but a film should be a film, and this one is a trailer for two other films, expensively disguised as a complete work.

With no money for distraction, this film simply sits down with its characters and listens to them, for ninety minutes, and the listening is riveting. There is no score to tell you how to feel, no production design to admire, no movement the budget could not afford. There is only writing and acting and attention, and the picture is a quiet reminder that those three things, and nothing else, have always been the actual art of cinema.

The picture braids a science-fiction premise into the structure of a chamber drama, and the combination, which sounds unpromising on paper, turns out to be inspired. The genre elements give the intimate story a strange new pressure, and the intimate story gives the genre elements a human weight they rarely carry. It is the rare hybrid in which each half genuinely needs the other, and the film could not exist as either thing alone.

There is a peculiar honesty about a film that knows exactly how silly it is and films itself in the long shadow of that fact. The new entry in the killer-shark-but-also-ghost subgenre is one such picture, and the practical effects team have built a marvellous puppet that wobbles in the right ways. The actors, several of whom I last saw doing better work in much smaller films, are clearly enjoying themselves. The picture is bad in all the ways a B-movie is supposed to be bad, which is to say it is good.

The film attempts something rare in mainstream animation: a story whose central conflict is internal rather than external. The protagonist's adversary is not a villain but a habit of thought, and the picture is structured around her gradual recognition of that pattern. The animation finds visual equivalents for the abstraction without ever lapsing into easy symbolism. By the end the picture has accomplished, in a children's animated feature, something many serious adult dramas attempt and fail at.

The debut suffers from the most common affliction of first features, which is the conviction that everything must be in it. The young director has poured a decade of ideas into a single ninety-minute film, and the picture is consequently overstuffed, lurching between tones and themes with the restless energy of someone who fears they may never get to make another. There is enough good material here for three films. Compressed into one, it exhausts rather than impresses.

subtopic: the overlooked release that deserves an audience
sentence: The picture has been quietly released to little notice, and the neglect is undeserved. It is a first feature, modest in scale and unflashy in execution, but it is built on a screenplay of real precision and a central performance that, in a fairer industry, would be the subject of conversation. Instead it will play to a few dozen people and disappear, and I want to register, at least, that it was here and it was good.

The debut arrives carrying a great deal of festival buzz, and the buzz has, as buzz tends to, oversold it. The film is a perfectly respectable first feature, competently made and sincerely felt, and in a quieter year it would attract a quieter and more accurate response. The young director has talent. The picture is promising. But promise is not the same thing as achievement, and the gap between the two has been papered over by a publicity apparatus that needed a discovery this season.

The picture arrived from Cannes carrying the kind of advance reputation that usually punishes a film when it finally screens for the rest of us. In this case the praise is largely deserved. The director's confidence is visible in every shot, the central performance is the most impressive of the year so far, and the structural risk of the second act — a sudden shift in narrator — pays off with a force that the cooler festival coverage did not quite capture. It will divide audiences. It will deserve to.

There is a scene late in this film, a single long take of the elderly lead simply listening to bad news, that contains more screen acting than most performers manage in an entire career. The actor does not reach for a single visible effect. He simply lets the news land, in real time, on a face that has been in front of cameras for sixty years, and the face does all of it, and the moment is unforgettable.

The film is set in 1740 but the screenwriter has clearly written it in 2024. Every character holds a recognisable modern opinion on every contested topic of the era, expressed with a fluency that nobody in the actual eighteenth century would have had access to. The costumes are immaculate; the heads inside them belong to graduates of contemporary universities. It is the kind of period drama that flatters its audience by allowing them to imagine themselves as the moral exceptions in every previous century.

subtopic: the polarising film that divided critics
sentence: I went into this film braced by the reviews for either a revelation or a catastrophe, and what I found was stranger and more interesting than either, a picture so committed to its own peculiar logic that it renders ordinary critical vocabulary almost useless. It cannot be graded on the usual scale. It can only be reckoned with, and the divided response is simply the sound of a great many critics reckoning, loudly and in public.

The planning sequences of this picture are some of the most pleasurable cinema of the year. The director understands that a heist's principal narrative engine is the explanation of itself, and she spends the first hour giving us a full geometric understanding of the building, the security, and the seven characters' individual capabilities. By the time the heist itself begins, the audience knows enough to anticipate the failures, and the film's pleasures consist almost entirely of those anticipations being broken and reformed in real time.

The film's twist, when it arrives, is so heavily foreshadowed that calling it a twist is generous, and the screenplay's evident pride in the reveal is the most embarrassing thing about the picture. The lead is doing solid work in an underwritten role. The supporting cast of handlers and double agents is interchangeable. The whole production has the air of a genre exercise assembled by people who have seen many spy films and understood none of them, and the result is two hours of glossy nothing.

subtopic: the studio film with troubled production history
sentence: The troubled production has yielded, against the odds, a genuinely interesting film, though not the film anyone set out to make. The chaos behind the camera seems to have loosened something, and the picture has a wild, unpredictable energy that a smoother shoot might have ironed out. It should not work. It frequently does not work. But when it works it is electric, and I would rather have this glorious mess than a competent film made in peace.

The picture is composed entirely of footage shot on expired film stock, and the chemical decay of the medium becomes the film's actual content. Images bloom and corrode, colours shift toward impossible registers, and the figures within the frames are gradually consumed by the deterioration of the material recording them. It is a film about mortality made by allowing the medium itself to die on screen, and it is one of the most genuinely moving experimental works I have encountered in years.

What this western understands is that the landscape is the antagonist. The human conflicts in the picture are real enough, but the director keeps pulling back to show the country itself, indifferent and enormous, and the people scratching at its surface seem smaller with every wide shot. By the final scene, the question of who wins the feud has come to feel almost beside the point, because the land will outlast all of them, and the film has made us feel that geological patience in our bones.

The film walks a genuinely difficult line, dramatising a subject around which any misstep would be disastrous, and it walks that line with remarkable poise. It neither flinches from the horror nor wallows in it. It gives the people at the centre of the story their full humanity rather than reducing them to the issue they represent, and that refusal of reduction is the picture's quiet, considerable moral achievement.

Half the appeal of this 1973 picture is the way it lets its actors disappear into a city. The location shooting is doing a tremendous amount of unobtrusive work — the diners are real diners, the apartment buildings are real apartment buildings, the cars on the streets are not extras but actual traffic. The protagonist's slow disintegration takes place inside this fabric and is the more affecting for it. Modern productions can no longer afford to shoot like this, which is, I think, a great loss.

The disaster film has a built-in problem, which is that spectacle has no memory, and this picture never solves it. The earthquake sequence is genuinely staggering, a twenty-minute set piece of collapsing infrastructure rendered with terrifying weight, and then the film must spend ninety minutes following survivors I have no reason to care about. The screenplay has assumed the catastrophe would do the emotional work. It cannot. A disaster film still needs people, and this one forgot to write any.

The picture follows a women's rowing crew through a single season, and the photography of the sport itself is extraordinary. The director has found camera positions on and around the water that make the physical labour legible in a way I have never quite seen before, the catch and drive of each stroke rendered with real clarity. The drama on land is more conventional, but every time the boat goes back on the river the film locates something close to the sublime, and that is enough.

Another war picture in which the bombing is dazzling, the brotherhood is moving, and the politics are quietly absent. The director knows how to stage a sortie and how to time a death, but he has no apparent interest in why any of these young men are flying these planes in the first place. The film leaves you with the texture of combat and none of its meaning, and after two and a half hours that absence becomes its own kind of statement.

The new entry in the absurdly long mutant-rabbit franchise is being released on premium streaming this week, and it is exactly as enjoyable as the previous six. The plot involves a corporate genetics laboratory, a small town with one diner, and a sheriff with a backstory. The kills are inventive, the mutant suit has been redesigned and is now somehow more endearing, and the picture clocks in at a brisk eighty-six minutes. There is more competent craft on display here than in many films four times its budget.

The picture has been shot on film rather than digitally, and the difference is not nostalgic affectation but a genuine aesthetic argument. The grain gives the image a living texture, a faint perpetual motion within every frame, and the way film handles the highlights, the soft bloom around a window or a lamp, lends the picture a warmth that digital crispness cannot replicate. The story is slight. The look is a sustained pleasure, and the look, here, is most of the point.

subtopic: child performance and family film reviews
sentence: The family film has become a debased category, a genre defined by what it carefully avoids rather than what it attempts, and this picture is a welcome rebuke to that timidity. It treats its young audience as intelligent. It allows its child characters to experience real fear, real loss, real moral difficulty, and it trusts that children can absorb a serious story. The result is a family film in the true sense, a film an actual family could watch together and afterwards have something to discuss.

There is a particular kind of biopic where the screenplay walks the lead from one famous photograph to the next, and this is one of those. We get the moment by the typewriter, the moment at the protest, the moment at the funeral, each lit and framed for the inevitable freeze frame. The actor is good. The picture is exhausting in the way museum gift shops are exhausting, and just as disposable.

There is a long sequence at the centre of this Edwardian picture in which two sisters fold linen for an entire afternoon, and almost nothing is said. The camera moves twice. The light shifts as the day passes. Everything that has gone wrong in the household, and everything that is about to go wrong, is contained in those minutes. It is the kind of confident filmmaking the prestige drama rarely allows itself any more, and I want to see more of it.

This is a musical for people who do not normally like musicals, which is both its great strength and its principal limit. The songs sit so naturally inside the dramatic scenes that you sometimes catch yourself, three lines in, realising the character has begun to sing. The film resists the form's standard punctuation — the held high note, the climactic key change, the chorus entry — and trades them for a quieter, more conversational kind of music. It is a beautiful experiment.

The film's central set piece — a forty-minute extended sequence inside the vault complex — is staged with such procedural clarity that it functions almost as a piece of silent cinema. There is virtually no dialogue, the score is replaced by the ambient sounds of the building, and the audience is given the geographic information it needs to follow every action in space. It is the best caper sequence since the heist film's last great revival, and it is worth the ticket on its own.

The recasting of the central role is the elephant in the cinema. The new actor is doing a respectful, slightly stiff impression of his predecessor, and the screenplay never quite finds a reason for him to make the part his own. The film around him is the same kind of capable-and-empty franchise picture this series has been making for a decade, only now with an extra layer of grief running through it that nobody on screen is permitted to acknowledge. It is sadder than it knows.

By the time the second hour begins, you can feel the screenplay running on the fumes of obligations. There are characters that have to be saluted, callbacks that have to be staged, and merchandise opportunities that have to be set up in close-up. The director, who is clearly a smart filmmaker, is doing his best to keep the picture alive in the gaps, but there are too many boxes to tick and not enough room for the kind of small unforced moments that made the first film special.

The picture's interest in adolescence is unusually free of nostalgia. The lead is allowed to be embarrassing, irritable, often quite stupid, and only intermittently appealing, which is exactly how adolescents behave in real life. The screenplay refuses to dignify her every choice with a structural payoff. She makes bad decisions and they remain bad decisions. By the end she has not learned a tidy lesson; she has merely become a slightly different person, which is what growing up actually feels like.

The film centres on two people in their sixties, both widowed, both wary, and the decision to age up the genre's central pairing turns out to be its most inspired choice. The obstacles to the romance are not the usual contrivances but the real accumulated weight of two long lives, and the screenplay treats that weight with respect. The picture is funny in a gentle, unhurried register, and it earns an ending that more frantic romantic comedies could never reach.

There is a real risk, in dramatising a subject this raw, of producing something that exploits the very pain it claims to examine, and this film does not entirely avoid the trap. There are sequences staged for an impact that tips over into spectacle, moments where the camera lingers in a way that serves the audience's appetite rather than the story's need. The picture is serious. It is also, in places, not as careful as its subject demanded.

subtopic: silent film and early cinema reviews
sentence: The picture is one of those early sound-era curiosities, made in the brief window when the cameras had to be locked inside soundproof booths, and the technical constraint has frozen the film into a stiff series of static tableaux. The actors stand in tight clusters around hidden microphones, declaiming. It is a fascinating historical document and a fairly tedious film, and the modern viewer is best served by watching it as evidence of a medium in the middle of forgetting everything it had learned.

Festival circuit catnip in all the wrong ways. The film is unembarrassed about its references — there are nods to Tarkovsky and Akerman in adjacent shots — but it doesn't earn its inheritance. The performances are mannered, the dialogue is opaque without being rich, and the running time is the kind of overlong that feels deliberate rather than necessary. I'll be surprised if anyone outside the festival circuit remembers it by autumn.

The film's score is a relentless act of emotional coercion. There is not a single moment in the picture that the music permits to be ambiguous. Sad scenes are scored sad, tense scenes are scored tense, and the orchestra arrives ahead of every feeling to instruct the audience exactly how to respond. A great score trusts the audience and leaves room for them. This one fills every silence with insistence, and the effect is less moving than bullying.

There's a courtroom scene about an hour in that quietly reorganises the film around itself, and from that moment the picture stops being a study of a marriage and starts being a study of how a marriage decides what it has been. The writing is dense without being airless, and the cinematography keeps choosing the unfashionable angle. It's a film that trusts you, and that's increasingly rare.

The remake of a foreign-language original commits the usual crime of the form, which is to sand away every specific cultural texture that made the source distinctive. The story has been relocated, the names have been changed, the strangeness has been smoothed into a generic familiarity, and what remains is a plot stripped of the context that gave it meaning. The original was about a particular place. The remake is about nowhere, and a film about nowhere is, finally, about nothing.

The picture stumbles, as so many do, at the third-act resolution, and the specific stumble is a failure of belief. The film does not believe its audience will accept an unhappy ending, and so it manufactures a hopeful one, a final scene of unearned reconciliation that contradicts everything the preceding two hours had honestly established. The film knew what its true ending was. It lost the courage to film it.

A first feature of startling formal ambition, and the ambition mostly pays off. The young director has built the picture around an unconventional structure, three timelines braided together without signposting, and a less confident newcomer would have lost control of it within twenty minutes. This one does not. The picture is demanding and occasionally cold, but it is the work of a real intelligence, and the technical assurance on display in a debut is genuinely uncommon.

The film has acquired a cult reputation almost entirely on the strength of one sequence — a fight in a roadside motel involving a chainsaw, a fire extinguisher and a startled raccoon — and the rest of it is not quite up to the legend. The performances are flat, the lighting is dim in a way that is mostly not artistic, and the pacing wobbles in the middle act. The motel sequence, however, is genuinely deranged in a way I cannot in good conscience disrecommend.

The most unsettling sequence in the film does not involve the supernatural at all. It is a fifteen-minute scene at a kitchen table, in which a mother and her adult son have a conversation about the empty bedroom upstairs, and neither of them looks at each other once. The director knows what kind of horror she is making, which is the kind that is mostly about families, and the genre flourishes are arranged around that knowledge rather than the other way round.

The prequel turns out to be the best film in the franchise, which is the rarest of outcomes. By going back to the protagonist's parents and the early years of the central conflict, the director has given the world a weight it never quite had when it was being built forward. The cast is uniformly good, but it is the costume and production design that does the heaviest lifting, making the world feel both familiar and previous, which is exactly the trick a prequel is supposed to land.

The film centres on a sixteen-year-old taking her first long bus journey alone, and the picture's small accumulated observations about that journey are extraordinary. The actors who play the strangers she meets along the way are uniformly excellent in roles that get five minutes of screen time apiece. The lead, in her debut, has the gift of doing almost nothing convincingly, which is the hardest thing a young actor can be asked to do, and the camera trusts her.

The film has been graded into a murky teal-and-orange palette so aggressively that the actors' faces have taken on the colour of corrosion. This is the house style of modern studio cinema, and I have come to loathe it. It flattens every location into the same dim sludge, drains the world of any colour that might distinguish one scene from another, and signifies, falsely, a kind of seriousness. The picture is not serious. It is merely badly lit, and proud of it.

subtopic: concert film and music documentary reviews
sentence: The music documentary covers the genre's familiar rise-and-fall arc, and it covers it competently, and I cannot pretend I needed to see it. The interviews are well-conducted, the archival footage is well-sourced, the narrative is well-shaped. But everything in the film is precisely what the form has trained us to expect, and the picture never once surprises, never finds the strange specific detail that would lift it out of the template. It is a perfectly professional act of telling us what we already knew.

subtopic: the studio film with troubled production history
sentence: It is well known that this film was taken away from its original director and finished by the studio, and the knowledge changes how one watches it, because the picture becomes a kind of detective puzzle. Here, you think, is the original vision, ambitious and strange. And here is where the studio intervened, flattening and explaining. The film is a battleground, and the studio, regrettably, won.

What the film does with its controversial material is, finally, to humanise it, and that is harder and rarer than the controversy around the picture suggests. It would have been easy to make this subject into an issue, a debate, a position to be argued. The director has instead made it into people, specific and flawed and impossible to reduce to a slogan, and in doing so she has made the only kind of film about this subject that was worth making.

It is the final film of the festival, and after a week of subtitled austerity it is, frankly, a relief. The picture is a bright, fast, unpretentious entertainment, and the gala audience visibly relaxed into it within the first ten minutes. I will not pretend it is the most important film I saw this week. But the programmers understood that a festival, like a meal, needs to end on something light, and they chose well.

Watching the recently restored print, you understand again why this 1974 picture has aged better than nearly any of its contemporaries. The studio-system polish has been replaced, scene by scene, with something rougher and more truthful — a courtyard rendered in actual sunlight, performers permitted to mumble and overlap, a screenplay that resists the closing reassurance the era's audiences had been taught to expect. It is the kind of film that argued, at the time, that the medium could grow up. Half a century on, it still does.

subtopic: child performance and family film reviews
sentence: The picture wants to be a heartwarming family adventure and is undone by a young lead who has plainly been directed to be adorable at all times. Every line is delivered with a calculated twinkle, every reaction is pitched for maximum audience sympathy, and the performance has the airless quality of a child being coached frame by frame. It is not the young actor's fault. It is a failure of direction, a failure to understand that a child on screen is most appealing when least aware of the camera.

The lead actress is doing the heavy lifting of an entire genre here, and she is more than equal to it. The screenplay asks her to be sympathetic and suspect in the same gesture, to make the audience care for a woman they cannot trust, and she finds a register of frayed warmth that holds both at once. The film around her is competent rather than inspired, but her performance is the kind that drags a middling thriller up into something worth seeing.

What I admired about this picture is its confidence to go without music. The director uses her score sparingly, perhaps four times across two hours, and the restraint means that when the orchestra finally does enter, the effect is overwhelming. The long unscored stretches teach the audience to listen to the film's actual sounds, the rooms and the weather and the breathing, and the eventual music lands like a held breath released. It is the most intelligent use of a film score I have heard in years.

The film is the rare mockumentary that actually has a point, and the point is sharper than the form usually allows. The fictional reality-television production company at the centre of the picture is a comic creation, but the satire about the labour conditions of its junior producers is real, and the picture earns the right to ask its audience to laugh because it has also done the harder work of asking them to be uncomfortable. It is a smarter film than its premise suggested.

subtopic: silent film and early cinema reviews
sentence: I had always been told this 1913 feature was a foundational work of the medium, and I went to the restored screening expecting to admire it dutifully and feel nothing. Instead I was genuinely moved. The film's storytelling is simpler than what would come later, but the simplicity has its own clarity, and the central performance, untrained by any later school of screen acting, has a directness that the more polished work of the following decades would partly lose. It is not a relic. It is a film.

The film arrives draped in the unmistakable costume of awards-season ambition, the weighty subject, the transformative performances, the tasteful restraint, and the costume fits a little too perfectly. Every element has been calibrated to a campaign rather than a story. The picture is accomplished, certainly, but it has the airless quality of a film made to be nominated, and I admired it the way one admires a well-filled-out form.

The film commits to its haunting with a patience that has gone out of fashion in this genre. The first scare arrives forty minutes in and is the better for the wait. The sound design is the real star — a low, almost subaudible hum under every domestic scene that you don't consciously hear until the silence that follows it. The lead performance is restrained to the point of stoicism, which is precisely what a film about grieving in a haunted house needed.

The film around him is forgettable, and I will likely forget it, but I will not forget the performance the old actor gives at its centre. There is a wisdom in the work that cannot be faked or taught, only earned across decades, and the picture's one undeniable achievement is that it gave a great performer, late in his life, a part large enough to hold all of it.

I have seen a great many spy films in which the tradecraft is decorative, a set of cool-looking behaviours signifying competence, and it is a pleasure to encounter one in which the tradecraft is the drama. This picture takes the time to show why an agent walks a particular route, why a particular café is chosen, what the cost of a single error in routine would be. The audience learns to think like a spy, and once we are thinking that way, the film's quiet crisis becomes genuinely terrifying.

There is a single musical idea in this film that justifies the whole picture. The composer has written a simple four-note motif, introduced quietly in the opening scene, and across two hours it is transformed, inverted, slowed, and finally, in the closing moments, resolved, and the resolution carries an emotional weight that the screenplay alone could never have reached. It is a master class in how a film score can tell a story underneath the story, and it deserves to be studied.

subtopic: the polarising film that divided critics
sentence: I have read the ecstatic reviews and the contemptuous ones, and I find myself unable to join either camp, which is, I suspect, the least interesting place to be on a film this divisive. The picture is genuinely ambitious and genuinely flawed, brilliant in stretches and inert in others, and my measured response feels like a failure to meet a film that demands a verdict rather than an assessment.

Everything wrong with this film is in its final twenty minutes. Strike them, and you would have a small, sharp, satisfying picture. As released, the film spends those final twenty minutes explaining itself, an exhausting sequence of expository confrontations in which characters tell each other, and us, what the preceding ninety minutes had already shown with perfect clarity. The third act does not advance the film. It annotates it.

Every psychological thriller now seems contractually obliged to deliver a third-act twist, and this one obliges so dutifully that the twist arrives drained of all surprise. The screenplay has spent ninety minutes laying a trail of obvious clues, and the eventual reveal is less a shock than the confirmation of a suspicion the film had practically printed in the programme. The lead is doing genuinely unsettling work. The structure she has been handed undermines her at every turn.

The picture follows the residents of a single apartment building over the course of a difficult year, and the building itself becomes the organising intelligence of the film. Characters pass each other on the stairs, overhear each other through the walls, and slowly, almost without noticing, become consequential to one another. The screenplay never forces the connections. It lets them accrue, and by the final scene the ensemble has become something like a community, which is harder to dramatise than it sounds.

The picture is set during a single tense week of a Cold War posting, and the period detail is exact without being fetishistic. The film understands that the great drama of espionage is bureaucratic, that the most consequential scenes happen when one officer decides whether to forward another officer's report, and it stages those small administrative betrayals with the gravity of combat. It is a slow, intelligent, deeply pessimistic film, and it is the best of its kind in a decade.

The ensemble film lives or dies by its balance, and this one is fatally unbalanced. Three of the storylines are vivid and well-acted; the other four are thin, and the film keeps dutifully returning to them out of structural obligation rather than dramatic need. Every cut away from the good material to the weak material is felt as a loss. A braver edit would have cut the picture down to the three stories that work, and it would have been a far better film.

What the cinematography achieves here is a genuine sense of place. The film is set in a single northern town, and the camera has been used to make us feel the specific quality of that town's light, the low winter sun, the long shadows, the particular grey of the sky. By the end of the film I felt I had visited a real location rather than a set, and that conviction is the cinematographer's quiet achievement, the kind that wins no awards because it never draws attention to itself.

What this remake gets right is that it has a genuine reason to exist. The original was a product of its moment, and its central premise has acquired, in the decades since, a wholly new set of resonances. The new film does not simply update the story; it re-thinks what the story now means, and the result is a picture in genuine dialogue with its source rather than merely indebted to it. It is the rare remake that justifies itself.

subtopic: child performance and family film reviews
sentence: The film rests almost entirely on the shoulders of its nine-year-old lead, and she carries it with a complete lack of strain. There is none of the precocious mugging that ruins so many child performances, none of the sense of a young actor performing cuteness for the camera. She simply is the character, attentive and uncertain and occasionally bored, and the director has had the wisdom to build the whole film around her unforced presence rather than around a plot.

The picture's central conceit, that the protagonist may be being slowly manipulated by everyone in her life, is the oldest trick in the psychological-thriller book, and the film knows it, and the knowing is what makes the picture work. The director plays openly with our genre expectations, letting us run ahead of the plot and then quietly demonstrating that our suspicion was itself a kind of manipulation. It is a film about paranoia that makes the audience complicit in the paranoia, and the effect is genuinely vertiginous.

The picture brings together a famous cast of a dozen recognisable faces, and the recognisability turns out to be the problem. Every time a beloved actor appears in a small role, the film stops dead for a beat of audience recognition, and the ensemble never quite coheres into a fictional world because it keeps reminding us it is a parade of stars. A genuine ensemble requires a degree of anonymity, a willingness to disappear into the group, and this glittering cast is constitutionally unable to disappear.

The director has decided that her musical numbers should be cut at the same frantic pace as the action sequences in her last picture, and the result is a film in which no song ever quite breathes. We see fragments of choreography that we know, from holding our attention to corners of the frame, was once continuous and beautiful, and we are denied the long takes that would have let us live inside it. It is a musical filmed by someone who does not entirely trust musicals.

subtopic: silent film and early cinema reviews
sentence: The 1925 picture is a reminder that the silent era's visual experimentation went far beyond anything the sound years would attempt for decades. There is a dream sequence in the second reel, accomplished through multiple exposures and hand-tinting, that is genuinely disorienting in the way the filmmaker plainly intended. The narrative is a slight thing, a melodrama of inheritance and disguise, but the picture's formal daring is undimmed by a hundred years, and it still feels like an experiment in progress.

What lifts this heist picture above its peers is its interest in what happens on the wrong side of the wall. The screenplay devotes nearly as much time to the security supervisor on the night shift as it does to the crew breaking in, and the picture's central tension is between two skilled professionals who never meet but are reacting to each other's decisions in real time. It is a structural elegance the genre does not often attempt, and the film is the more interesting for the attempt.

The film tackles its difficult subject without offering the audience the consolations the subject usually comes wrapped in. There is no redemptive arc, no uplift, no sense that the suffering has been made to mean something. The director has refused all of it, and the refusal is harsh and honest and correct, because the false comfort would have been a lie, and a lie about this particular subject would have been unforgivable.

Everything about this romantic comedy has been assembled from a kit. The meet-cute happens in a coffee shop, the best friend exists solely to deliver advice, the rival suitor is conspicuously charmless, and the grand gesture takes place at an airport. The two leads are appealing performers stranded in roles that ask nothing of them but to be appealing. The film is not painful to watch, exactly. It is simply the cinematic equivalent of a postcard, pleasant and immediately forgotten.

There is a long lead performance at the centre of this contender, the kind that involves a visible physical transformation and a great deal of suffering, and it is being discussed as a certainty for the major prizes. The performance is, in fact, very good. It is also exactly the performance the season rewards every year, and I found myself wishing the actor had been given something subtler to do than to be obviously, awardably excellent.

The dystopia in this film is so over-designed it becomes camp. Every surface is wet, every uniform is grey, every loudspeaker is bolted to a wall at the wrong angle. The director clearly loves the genre's furniture and has assembled an entire museum of it. What is missing is anyone living inside the museum. The protagonist's predicament is plot, not lived experience, and the picture feels less like a novel than like a really expensive piece of concept art.

subtopic: the film that improves on a second viewing
sentence: I suspect this film will be substantially reappraised in a few years, once audiences have had the chance to see it twice. On a single viewing it is easy to mistake its patience for emptiness and its ambiguity for evasion. A second viewing dispels both impressions completely. The picture is dense, deliberate, and fully in command of its effects, and it has simply been released into a culture that no longer watches films twice.

A film entirely composed of moments that should not work — the practical-effects helicopter that is obviously a model, the gore that exceeds any reasonable amount of viable blood for a single human body, the romantic subplot between two characters who have spoken three sentences to each other — and that, by some mysterious chemistry, almost entirely does. Cult cinema lives in these gaps between what filmmakers can afford and what they decide to attempt, and this picture sits comfortably in the better half of that tradition.

The reboot makes the smart decision to keep its connection to the original loose, taking the premise as a starting point rather than a template, and the freedom serves it well. The new film tells its own story, finds its own tone, and trusts the audience to appreciate the franchise without needing it slavishly reproduced. It will disappoint the purists who wanted a faithful echo. It will reward everyone else, because it is, against the odds, a genuinely good film in its own right.

subtopic: screen adaptation of a stage play
sentence: The play has been opened up for the screen with such enthusiasm that the thing the stage version did best has been mislaid in the process. On stage, the single confined set was the point; the characters were trapped together, and the audience felt the walls. The film, anxious about cinematic stillness, keeps inventing reasons for the cast to walk outside, and every exterior scene drains a little more pressure from the room. The performances remain superb. The adaptation has misunderstood its source.
